title: Focal Length
description: Lying on the pavement between towers, looking straight up. Turn the zoom ring from 24 mm to 10 mm: at the long end it is mostly cumulus, the towers creeping in at the corners; as it widens they lean in from the edges and the corners stretch like a real rectilinear ultra-wide, and below 16 mm the drawing eases toward stereographic so the towers bend into spokes round the sky. The camera never moves, so nothing about the perspective changes, only how much of it the lens takes in and how it is drawn. One 360 capture, projected exactly through r = f k tan(theta / k), developed like daylight negative film.
intent: Summer-film genre spec, idea 6 (Focal Length), adapted to a worm's-eye view: herb's reference 2 (factory/reality/herb-refs/2-wormseye-skyscrapers.png), towers converging into a cumulus sky, reached by turning a zoom ring rather than tilting. Projection family from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisheye_lens#Mapping_function

sources.author: Andreas Mischok
sources.note: 16K HDR, the towers and street. Reprojected to a zenith cap (azimuthal equidistant, 95 degrees) and re-lit by the new sky's sun: facade normals from the floor lines give each face a sun incidence, sun-facing faces get about a stop of warm-neutral light, faces turned away go toward near-black with a little skylight blue, and cranes stay backlit silhouettes. Then regraded on the exported plates (regrade_towers.py) toward herb's ref 2: shade faces taken down 1.1 stops and tinted cobalt (212 degrees), their glass a mirror of what is across the street: each pane reflects, through a teal coating, about 30% of the plate in its mirror direction (the elevation kept, the azimuth mirrored in the face's normal, raised for the parallax of a ray that leaves the facade rather than the camera), so the crowns and the upper floors carry the cumulus and the lower ones the towers opposite, modulated by each pane's own texture; sun-facing faces lifted 0.7 stop under the clouds' own soft shoulder, with the sun map read from the faces' existing warmth; on them only the stone and the mullions take warm gold (35 to 38 degrees), while the glass, keyed from the capture's own cool chroma, keeps its grey-teal hue with some skylight mixed in, so teal glass and warm stone sit side by side. Last, clone_cap.py takes out three distractions: the crown of a distant tower that the 10 mm frame clipped into a floating fragment at its top edge (replaced with sky fitted to its surroundings), the lettering of a news ticker on the curved tower, and a crane jib floating in the sky past the stone tower's crown (inpainted from the clear sky round it). Then face_cap.py makes two clean-3D repairs on the curved glass tower at the lower left: its shaded flank, which the mirror pass had smeared into soft cloud blobs with a pale streak down the arris, is rebuilt from the native 16K capture sampled straight into each plate's geometry (area-averaged), so its mullion and floor grid carries on from the lit face at full sharpness, toned to the old flank's smooth profile in cobalt-teal; its arris is redrawn on the capture's own vertical edge and choked 2.5 px, with the uncovered strip filled from the clean sky beyond; and the rooftop and crane jib that poked in at the bottom-centre edge of the 10 mm frame become sky (a push-pull fill from the clear sky round them, with its own fine noise), ending past the frame on a roofline that never shows. Last, glass_faces.py gives the two towers right of the sky the same rebuild: the dark grid tower at right-middle and the curved glass tower above it, whose rounded crown and canopy span the top-right of the 14 and 20 mm frames, had taken the mirror pass as grey-blue blotches and smears that dissolved their window grid. Both are resampled from the native 16K capture straight into each plate's geometry (area-averaged), so the stone frame and window grid of the one and the structural fins of the other stay sharp all the way across; the body light is one smooth profile down each tower in the curved tower's flank cobalt, pulled toward teal, with the capture's pane texture compressed hard; and the glass carries one coherent mirror of the sky alone (the plate with its towers pushed out and filled from the sky round them), read in each face's mirror direction and weighted by Schlick Fresnel for that incidence, instead of per-pane reflections. The fins are kept as long ridges of the capture (a width-selective top-hat, small pieces dropped), and where the curved tower's glass reflects the grid tower opposite, only straight runs survive, so that reflection does not come back as a lattice.

sources.author: Greg Zaal (original), Jarod Guest (sky edits)
sources.note: 16K HDR cumulus sky, set in behind the towers with a luminance matte (sky at infinity, so the composite is geometrically exact), rotated so the sun sits behind a tower, and regraded as clear sky plus cloud light on a smooth, dithered ramp from cyan 200 degrees at the horizon to cobalt 212 degrees at the zenith, saturation capped so no gap goes ultramarine. The cumulus is then relit by the same sun: a cloud matte from the unmixed cloud share, isolated stray puffs dropped, the top of the cloud luminance range pushed toward warm-neutral #FFF4E6 under a soft per-channel shoulder that rolls off near 245, the lower half pulled toward skylight blue (208 degrees, S 0.25), and every edge given a thin translucent fringe of the local sky colour; regrade_towers.py then split-tones every cloud pixel on one smooth logistic key of its log luminance (centred on the 75th percentile, 0.28 stop wide, no hard threshold): warm-neutral #FFF4E6 on the tops, skylight blue 208 degrees (S 0.36) below, at the pixel's own luminance. The matte is unmixed at true coverage, then choked and feathered about 2.5 px round the tower crowns. Stored as scene light / 2, sRGB webp: a 4096 cap to 95 degrees and a native-resolution 4096 inset (the centre of the 8192 cap) of the centre 47.5 degrees, which holds the whole frame at 20 mm.
